notes: AG reference for unduly lenient glassing sentence; Court of Appeal increased total custody and clarified s35/36 powers.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref No 32: unduly lenient sentence for bottle-glassing and affray
key_facts: A 21-year-old offender pleaded guilty to section 18 wounding with intent after deliberately breaking a beer bottle and striking the victim in the neck during a street confrontation.
He received two years' detention in a young offender institution for the section 18 offence and a concurrent twelve months for a separate affray committed while on bail.
Aggravating features included use of a deliberately broken bottle, unprovoked attack, recent release from a 30-month sentence for unlawful wounding, and commission while on licence.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient under section 36 of the 1988 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 for leave to refer unduly lenient Crown Court sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; the section 18 sentence was increased to two years with twelve months consecutive for affray and nine months for the unexpired portion of the earlier sentence, totalling three years and nine months' detention.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 36 reference the Court of Appeal may quash any sentence passed in the proceedings and has all Crown Court sentencing powers, including ordering consecutive sentences for either-way offences and requiring service of an unexpired licence term under section 116, despite the offender's double-jeopardy discount.
legal_issues: Whether the two-year section 18 sentence was unduly lenient for deliberate glassing
Whether the Court of Appeal could alter the affray sentence where the offence was not triable only on indictment
Whether the court could make a section 116 order where the recorder had not exercised that power
Appropriate tariff for deliberate bottle-glassing offences

Attorney-General's Reference No 14 of 2000 (R v Boffey) [2000] 1 Cr App R(S) 55
Attorney-General's Reference No 25 of 2002 (R v Mentlak) [2003] 1 Cr App R(S) 130

notes: Section 288 planning appeal; Sullivan J upheld SoS refusal of rural management training centre at Purley Chase.

enrichment.short_title: Macepark v SoS: planning refusal for Purley Chase training centre upheld
key_facts: The claimant sought to quash the Secretary of State's refusal of planning permission for a large hotel, management training and leisure complex at Purley Chase Golf Club near Atherstone.
An inspector recommended grant subject to conditions and a section 106 agreement, but the Secretary of State disagreed on development plan, PPG 6, PPG 7 and PPG 13 grounds.
The inspector considered Structure Plan policy I.8 the dominant tourism policy, but the Secretary of State accorded it less weight than general urban-focused policies.
The Secretary of State rejected the claim that a rural location was operationally necessary for a corporate management training centre.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against a called-in planning refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Secretary of State's refusal was lawful and his planning judgments on development plan conflict, rural location, sequential approach and car parking were within his discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Where development plan policies pull in different directions the decision-maker may accord differing weight to user-specific and general locational policies; disagreement with an inspector's planning judgment on rural operational need, PPG 6 sequential compliance and PPG 13 travel impacts does not require quashing if adequately reasoned.
legal_issues: Whether the proposal was generally in accordance with the development plan
Whether a rural location was operationally required for a management training centre
Compliance with PPG 6 sequential approach and demonstrated need for leisure facilities
Whether conflict with PPG 13 was mitigated by a green travel plan and shuttle bus
Weight to be given to the extant 1996 fallback permission
linked_authorities: R (Cummins) v Camden London Borough Council [2001] EWHC Admin 116
R v Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council ex parte Milne [2001] 81 P&CR 27

confidence.notes: Detailed planning reasoning though many subsidiary PPG points were treated as non-decisive.

notes: Colman J dismissed s68 remission application in GENCON demurrage dispute over contaminated cargo holds.

enrichment.short_title: Alphapoint v Rotem: section 68 demurrage award upheld after hold contamination
key_facts: Shipowners claimed demurrage under a GENCON voyage charter after barley residue contaminated phosphate, potash and salt cargoes at Eilat, suspending loading for about a week.
The arbitrators found the holds were not ready when notice of readiness was accepted and deducted the cleaning period from demurrage under clause 25 and by way of damages for breach of clause 23(b).
Owners argued estoppel from acceptance of notice of readiness and that charterers benefited when another vessel, the VANA, used the vacated berth.
Leave to appeal under section 69 was refused before the section 68 application was heard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application under section 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to remit a final demurrage award, heard together with a refused section 69 leave application.
enrichment.outcome: Section 68 application dismissed; no serious irregularity causing substantial injustice was established and the award was not remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Acceptance of notice of readiness may start laytime without waiving a separate claim for damages for unclean holds or crew failure under clause 25; an arbitrator may reject speculative countervailing points on quantum where charterers' entitlement to deduct time under clause 25 does not depend on proof of damages.
legal_issues: Whether charterers were estopped from relying on unclean holds after accepting notice of readiness
Whether the arbitrators failed to consider the estoppel and partial-loading cleaning evidence
Whether the arbitrators improperly raised their own VANA demurrage point without notice
Relationship between sections 68 and 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996
linked_authorities: The HELLE SKOU [1976] 2 Lloyd's Rep 205
Annie Fox v Wellfair [1981] 2 Lloyd's Rep 514

confidence.notes: Arbitrators' reasoning and Colman J's analysis of clause 23(b) and clause 25 are explicit.

notes: Deemed section 109 consent for smaller kiosk application; Agency could not refuse to entertain valid application.

enrichment.short_title: Amberley House: deemed Water Resources Act consent for culvert kiosk application
key_facts: The claimant built a 42 sqm retail kiosk over a culverted section of the River Lavant in Chichester without section 109 consent and received an enforcement notice requiring removal.
Two section 109 applications were submitted: one for a smaller 28 sqm kiosk (Building A) with planning permission, and one retrospective application for Building B.
The Environment Agency refused to entertain either application, treating both as impermissible retrospective consents.
Application 1 sought consent for a different, smaller structure for which planning permission had been granted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review seeking declarations and mandatory orders requiring the Environment Agency to determine section 109 applications.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; application 1 was a valid section 109 application and, consent having been neither given nor refused within two months, was deemed granted under section 110(2)(b); the Agency conceded it would not enforce against the existing structure.
enrichment.ratio: A section 109 application for a different structure from one already erected without consent is not necessarily a retrospective application; where the Agency refuses to entertain a valid application it does so at its peril and section 110(2)(b) deems consent granted after two months.
legal_issues: Whether retrospective section 109 applications are permitted
Whether application 1 was invalid because a larger kiosk already stood on the site
Effect of section 110(2)(b) where the Agency disputes validity of an application
Interaction between section 109 enforcement powers and subsequent valid applications

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and declaration are clearly reasoned; merits of consent not decided.

notes: Rent review s68 remission granted where arbitrator double-counted onerous lease term discounts.

enrichment.short_title: St George's v Gemini: rent review award remitted for unargued lease discounts
key_facts: An arbitrator determined the reviewed rent of lower ground floor offices at 1 Knightsbridge at £472,624 using a third-floor discount methodology.
Both valuers agreed the third-floor comparable was the primary evidence but disputed the discount percentage; the arbitrator applied 60% plus further 15% deductions for onerous lease terms.
Those onerous lease term discounts had been used by the tenant's expert only in a separate comparables exercise, not in the third-floor discount method.
The landlord contended the arbitrator introduced a hybrid methodology without opportunity to respond, causing double counting.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 68(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996 to remit a rent review award for serious irregularity.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; serious irregularity under section 33 caused substantial injustice and the award was remitted in whole for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: An arbitrator commits serious irregularity where he adopts a valuation methodology mixing the parties' approaches and applies onerous lease term discounts not put in issue on the agreed third-floor discount basis, depriving a party of a fair opportunity to show double counting.
legal_issues: Whether onerous lease term discounts were in the arena for decision
Whether the arbitrator could deploy evidence differently from both valuers
Application of Checkpoint and Warborough principles to paper arbitrations
Whether substantial injustice was shown on the rent figure

Warborough Investments Limited v S Robinson & Sons (Holdings) Limited [2003] EWCA Civ 751
Zermalt Holdings SA v Nu-Life Upholstery Repairs Limited [1985] 2 EGLR 14

notes: Vexatious litigant's case management appeal dismissed; transfer to county court and costs upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Kohanzad v Derbyshire Police: vexatious litigant's case management appeal dismissed
key_facts: Mr Kohanzad, subject to a vexatious litigant order, sued Derbyshire Police for alleged assault by officers on 6 May 2002, claiming about £5 million damages.
At a case management conference held in his absence while he was in prison, HHJ Orrell transferred the claim to Derby County Court and vacated the trial date.
The judge ordered the claimant to pay £450 costs of the hearing by 19 December 2003.
The claimant had written belatedly requesting an adjournment but gave no clear notice to the defendant's solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from case management orders made at a conference on 26 November 2003 in the Derby District Registry.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; transfer to the County Court was a sensible case management decision and the costs order was within the judge's discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Routine case management decisions including transfer of a modest-value personal injury claim to the County Court and costs orders against a litigant who belatedly sought to vacate a fixture will not be interfered with on appeal absent demonstrated error of discretion.
legal_issues: Whether transfer to the County Court was inappropriate given the pleaded damages
Whether orders should not have been made in the claimant's absence
Whether the defendant should have paid costs because the claimant was in prison
Scope of the Court of Appeal to entertain criminal proceedings complaints

confidence.notes: Disposal is clear though detailed reasons for the costs order were not before the court.

notes: Burnton J refused wide without-notice injunctions in Chinese forex introducing broker dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Marketmaker v CMC: interim injunctions refused in China forex agency dispute
key_facts: Chinese introducing broker companies claimed CMC wrongfully terminated agency agreements and sought wide without-notice injunctions restraining denial of agency and breaches of Chinese forex law.
Fulford J granted limited interim relief on 7 June 2004, but Stanley Burnton J refused continuation at a contested hearing with extensive documentary evidence.
Written Obair and FXT IB agreements prohibited the claimants holding themselves out as CMC agents; alleged informal side agreements were unsupported by contemporaneous documents.
The claimants sought unprecedented orders restraining defendants from denying agency and from trading in breach of disputed Chinese regulatory advice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Return date on without-notice interim injunction applications in a commercial dispute over forex introducing broker arrangements in China.
enrichment.outcome: All further injunctive relief refused; no arguable cause of action supported the agency or Chinese illegality injunctions, and informal agreements were not triable issues.
enrichment.ratio: An injunction restraining a defendant from denying agency requires a pleaded cause of action and cannot be granted in vague terms infringing free speech; an English court should not grant quia timet relief requiring compliance with disputed foreign criminal law absent a clear domestic legal basis.
legal_issues: Whether an arguable cause of action existed for an agency injunction
Whether alleged informal agreements created binding contracts
Whether an implied term required CMC to comply with Chinese law
Appropriateness of injunctive relief based on disputed foreign criminal law
Particularisation requirements for confidential information injunctions
linked_authorities: The Siskina [1979] AC 210
Ocular Sciences Ltd v Aspect Vision Care Ltd [1997] RPC 289

notes: PAT appeal allowed on article 5 reasonable doubt test after Porton Down mustard/GF gas tests.

enrichment.short_title: Roche v MoD: war pension appeal remitted after Porton Down gas tests

statutes_considered.title: Naval, Military and Air Forces Etc (Disablement and Death) Service Pensions Order 1983

key_facts: Former Sapper Thomas Roche volunteered for mustard gas and GF nerve gas tests at Porton Down in 1962-63 and later developed chronic obstructive airways disease.
He claimed a war disability pension attributing COAD to the tests, but the Pensions Appeal Tribunal rejected the appeal finding no reliable evidence of causal link.
Professor Hay's expert answers repeatedly stated he could not exclude the possibility of a link but also described it as unlikely and ruled out GF as a cause.
A section 10 Crown Proceedings Act certificate had barred civil proceedings, making the pension scheme the primary compensation route.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law with permission under section 6 of the Pensions Appeals Tribunals Act 1943 from a PAT decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Tribunal erred in treating Professor Hay's evidence as excluding reasonable doubt and the COAD claim was remitted for rehearing.
enrichment.ratio: Under article 5(4) of the 1983 Order the benefit of reasonable doubt must be given to the claimant where reliable evidence raises it; cherry-picking unequivocal passages from an expert who also stated possibilities cannot be excluded is inconsistent with that test.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'reliable evidence' and 'reasonable doubt' under article 5(4)
Whether the PAT correctly applied the burden under article 5(2)
Proper interpretation of Professor Hay's equivocal expert evidence
Relevance of absent epidemiological follow-up studies
linked_authorities: Busmer [2004] EWHC 29 Admin
Westcott v Secretary of State for Social Services (11 December 1987)
Dickinson v Minister of Pensions [1953] QB 226

confidence.notes: Legal error identified clearly though causation on remittal remains contested.

notes: Landmark ECHR challenge to gross negligence manslaughter rejected; doctors' convictions upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Misra: gross negligence manslaughter compatible with ECHR
key_facts: Two senior house officers failed to diagnose and treat severe post-operative infection in Sean Phillips after knee surgery, leading to death from toxic shock syndrome.
Expert evidence showed classic signs of sepsis were ignored for days; blood test results were never checked and appropriate antibiotics were not given in time.
Both doctors were convicted of manslaughter by gross negligence and received suspended sentences.
The trial judge certified whether gross negligence manslaughter complies with Articles 6 and 7 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with certified question on ECHR compatibility of gross negligence manslaughter, plus application to admit fresh statistical evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; gross negligence manslaughter is sufficiently certain under Article 7 and compatible with Article 6, following R v Adomako; fresh statistical evidence refused.
enrichment.ratio: The ingredients of manslaughter by gross negligence are clearly defined: breach of duty of care exposing the victim to an obvious risk of death, grossly falling below proper standards; the jury's assessment that conduct was gross and consequently criminal is a fact-specific evaluation, not impermissible circularity.
legal_issues: Whether gross negligence manslaughter lacks certainty contrary to Article 7 ECHR
Whether jury directions involving 'criminal' conduct violate Article 6 fair trial rights
Whether manslaughter by gross negligence requires mens rea after R v G
Whether the risk for gross negligence manslaughter is death or serious injury
Admissibility of fresh statistical evidence on causation under section 23
linked_authorities: R v Adomako [1995] 1 AC 171
R v G and Another [2004] 1 AC 1034
Andrews v DPP [1937] AC 576

confidence.notes: Comprehensive appellate treatment of Adomako principles and ECHR compatibility.

notes: IR35 appeal dismissed; Park J rejected substitution and mutuality challenges to deemed employment.

enrichment.short_title: Usetech v HMRC: IR35 applies to Pro-Engineer contractor via NES agency
key_facts: Mr Hood provided Pro-Engineer design services to ABB through his one-man company Usetech, contracted via agency company NES under upper and lower level contracts.
HMRC decided IR35 applied, treating Usetech's receipts as deemed employment income of Mr Hood with ABB as notional employer.
The Usetech/NES contract contained a standard substitution clause, but the NES/ABB contract was solely for Mr Hood's personal services.
Mr Hood worked about 58 hours per week at ABB's Aberdeen premises for 17 months under arrangements closely resembling employment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on points of law from a Special Commissioner's decision dismissing IR35 appeals for income tax and NICs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the hypothetical direct contract between Mr Hood and ABB would not have included a meaningful substitution right and contained sufficient mutuality, so Schedule 12 applied.
enrichment.ratio: For IR35 purposes the notional worker-client contract is constructed from all relevant arrangements including the agency/end-user contract; a substitution clause binding only the service company and agency does not enter the hypothetical contract where the end user contracted specifically for the named individual.
legal_issues: Whether the hypothetical Hood/ABB contract would include a substitution provision
Whether substitution clauses prevent a contract being one of employment
Whether lack of mutuality of obligation excluded deemed employment
Effect of minimum hours provisions in the NES/ABB contract
Construction of Finance Act 2000 Schedule 12 paragraph 1
linked_authorities: Ready Mixed Concrete (South East) Ltd v Minister of Pensions [1968] 2 QB 497
Express and Echo Publications Ltd v Tanton [1999] IRLR 367
Synaptek Ltd v Young [2003] STC 543
